prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, whose magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms enabled frequency measurement at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I still place the optical lattice clock first, and the colleagues' openings have strengthened rather than weakened that view. It is a clean idea (trap neutral atoms at the magic wavelength so that the clock transition is not shifted by the trapping light, while thousands of atoms are interrogated Doppler- and recoil-free) that produced a qualitatively new capability: clocks at the 1e-18 level, tested against each other in many laboratories. What I value most as a theorist who has to compute such systematics is that the measurements can be confronted with theory: magic wavelengths, blackbody-radiation shifts and polarizabilities are exactly the quantities atomic many-body theory is asked to deliver, and the agreement between independent clocks says the understanding is real. It is also physically fundamental: gravitational redshift resolved over centimetres, limits on drifting constants and on ultralight dark matter, and a redefinition of the second. Four of the five members who ranked it put it in their top three, three of them first, and the reasons they give (reproduction by JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, SYRTE, PTB and others; a two-name credit that fits the record) are scientific rather than merely a matter of habit. A prize of two people, Katori for the concept and first realization and Ye for taking the lattice clock to record accuracy and stability, is compact and leaves the remaining prize slot structure unconstrained.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is incrementalism. The 2005 prize (Hall, Hansch) gave us the frequency comb that makes optical clocks countable, and the 2012 prize (Haroche, Wineland) honoured control of single quantum systems and the ion optical clock. A committee could say that the lattice clock is the best instrument in an already-honoured lineage, and that its fundamental payoffs (a redefined second, a dark-matter or varying-constant signal) are promised rather than delivered. Second, attribution has a real tail: the SYRTE, PTB and NIST groups, Ludlow, Takamoto, Hinkley and others built much of the systematics programme, and Ye's name rests partly on record accuracy and many-body clock physics rather than on the original idea. Third, I am relying on my own recollection of the priority history and the 1e-18 figures, so I would want these checked against the published record before a final ballot.

responses.point: Pearce ranks the lattice clock first as an instrument-builder's achievement, but flags that it belongs to the same lineage as the 2005 and 2012 prizes and that Ye's credit must be balanced against other clock pioneers.
responses.response: I take the incrementalism worry seriously, but I think it is answered by what is new in kind. The comb measured optical frequencies; the ion clock showed control of one quantum system; the lattice clock combines Doppler- and recoil-free interrogation with large atom numbers, which is what makes 1e-18 stability reachable in hours and opens the gravitational-redshift and many-body clock physics. On Ye I agree there is a fairness question, but Katori's concept plus Ye's demonstration of record accuracy is the cleanest allocation the record offers, and I would not add a third clock name without evidence that someone else shaped the field to the same degree. I do not think our shared first place is evidence of merit by itself; we should test it against the 2005 and 2012 citations in the open.

responses.point: Kroll also puts the lattice clock first and puts atom interferometry (B015) second, arguing that new measurement techniques open new ways of observing nature, though he concedes that Chu's absence weakens the trio.
responses.response: I agree on the clock, and with the principle, but I would qualify his second choice. Atom interferometry is a beautiful application of matter-wave coherence and it speaks to the quantum-classical boundary I care about, yet his own attribution note shows the problem: Chu is central to light-pulse interferometry and is already a laureate for cooling, and Pritchard, Kasevich and Bordé do not split the credit cleanly. For me that is a reason to keep B015 below the trapped-ion and cavity-QED candidates until the claim of each name is documented. The clock has the opposite property: the credit is nearly unambiguous and the performance is quantitative.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks twisted bilayer graphene first: a theory-led prediction of magic-angle flat bands followed by experimental discovery of correlated insulators and superconductivity, opening moire quantum materials.
responses.response: This is a serious candidate and I defer to colleagues in condensed matter on its physics. The prediction-then-discovery structure is the kind of thing I admire, and it was reproduced by many groups within a few years, so my usual worry about single-measurement claims does not apply. My reservations are about maturity and attribution, both of which he himself raises: the origin of the superconductivity is unresolved, and the first author of the decisive experiments (Yuan Cao) and earlier band-structure theorists are outside the three names. I would not call the unresolved mechanism disqualifying, since the phenomenon is robust, but I would want the committee to be sure the citation can be written so as to credit the discovery of correlated states without claiming an explanation. If condensed-matter colleagues judge that credit is settled, I could place it ahead of the cold-atom and cavity-QED options.

responses.point: Mehlig argues for defect-mediated two-dimensional melting and the hexatic phase (B051), a simple general mechanism whose half of the story was not covered by the 2016 topological-phase-transition prize.
responses.response: I find the argument for generality attractive, and I accept that five decades of confirmation is more than most candidates can claim. I am not the right person to weigh the statistical-mechanics literature, but his own caveat gives me pause: simulations show first-order melting in some systems, notably hard disks, so the cleanest statement of what was discovered depends on the system. A citation would need to say what is universal and what is not. I would also ask whether recognising this soon after Kosterlitz and Thouless would read as a second prize for one idea. These are questions for him and the condensed-matter members; I do not rank it highly only because I cannot test it, not because I see a flaw.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED (B042) first as the readout, coupling and control architecture of superconducting qubits, while openly noting his closeness to the field and the allocation problem around Girvin.
responses.response: I respect that he declares his closeness to the field, and I agree that circuit QED is the solid-state descendant of atomic cavity QED, which is why I rank it highly in principle. My difficulty is timing and distinctness: it follows the 2025 prize on superconducting circuits closely, and a prize in the same area a year later would, I think, be hard to defend to the wider community when other mature areas are waiting. The four-name attribution (Blais, Girvin, Wallraff, Schoelkopf) also does not fit within three. I would keep it as a strong alternative but not as my first choice this year.

uncertainties: Whether the committee judges the lattice clock sufficiently distinct from the 2005 (frequency comb) and 2012 (single quantum systems) prizes.

Priority history between Katori's concept and the contemporaneous work of other clock groups, and whether Ye's credit rests on the concept or on the record-accuracy implementation; I have not verified this against the primary record.
Whether the committee wants to wait for the formal redefinition of the second before recognising the clock.
Credit allocation for the Cirac-Zoller candidates (B036, B004) if the committee prefers a quantum-information or quantum-simulation prize, since the same theory pair appears twice.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for the credited names Katori and Ye. My close collaborators (L'Huillier, Keller's group, Dahlstrom, Argenti, Schuch, Indelicato) are not credited on any shortlisted ballot, though I work in the same broad field of atomic precision physics and have a general interest in precision atomic theory, which I disclose.
